sections.summary: Introduces the extended mind question and the argument from extended cognition. It uses the Tetris mental-rotation cases to show that external physical manipulation can parallel internal cognitive processing, distinguishes epistemic from pragmatic action, and develops active externalism as a coupled-system view. The unit then contrasts this with Putnam/Burge passive externalism and argues that external features in a coupled system play an active, ineliminable causal role.
sections.title: Extended Cognition and Active Externalism

sections.summary: Continues from the Scrabble-tile example into broader cognitive-science support, then addresses the portability objection. It argues that reliable coupling with external resources can make calculators, notebooks, neural modules, evolved environmental dependencies, and language part of the basic package of cognitive resources rather than mere add-ons.
sections.title: Reliable Coupling and the Portability Objection

sections.summary: Extends the argument from cognitive processing to belief. The Inga and Otto comparison shows that Otto's notebook can play the role ordinarily played by biological memory, so Otto's belief can be partly constituted by the notebook. Twin Otto then shows how external features can alter belief content, and the unit contrasts this active external role with Putnam/Burge cases.
sections.title: Extended Belief: Otto and Inga

sections.summary: Defends extended belief against objections concerning reliability, access, perception, and phenomenology. It argues that the differences between Otto and Inga are shallow, that constancy, direct availability, automatic endorsement, and past endorsement make notebook entries belief-like, and that even if one rejects occurrent-belief requirements, Otto's notebook has the relevant dispositions.
sections.title: Objections to Extended Belief

sections.summary: Explores the outer limits of the extended mind. It examines criteria for extended belief, puzzle cases, socially extended cognition, language as a cognitive extension, and the extended self. It concludes with the moral and social consequences of treating agents as spread into the world and of usurping the hegemony of skin and skull.
sections.title: Beyond the Outer Limits: Social Extension, Self, and Consequences
